A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Additionally, we explore how the packing of nuclei
at the upper surface influences migration speed, suggest alternative mechanisms for controlling entry and exit points
from the cell cycle, and propose a means of examining time-dependent variation in retinal IKNM speed. By making
these concepts more precise and quantifiable, we hope to contribute to a broader understanding of how neural diversity
is generated in this system. By sharing our imaging approaches and data analysis strategies, we aim to facilitate further
exploration of retinal IKNM in other organisms and developmental contexts. By revealing the dynamic, migrating cell
nucleus as more than just a passive entity waiting for exit points from the cell cycle, we hope to initiate a shift in how
we view this phenomenon and to encourage investigation of the nucleus as an active component that contributes to its
own movement patterns. Furthermore, we contend that careful consideration of data collection schedules is vital when
designing and interpreting experiments involving the analysis of freely moving, densely packed objects within a two- or
three-dimensional space. Lastly, we contemplate the broader applicability of these findings to other complex, dynamically
changing systems that involve the coordinated movement of numerous objects in an unstructured environment.  As a result of studying this specific system, we have developed novel approaches for high-speed, multi-scale imaging in live organisms during critical periods of development, along with a range of advanced data analysis strategies for processing intricate biological data sets. Strong partnerships can drive the success of universities through collaborative research, hiring top talent, and attracting significant funding. To gain insight into the nature of these partnerships, we examined the networks of 37 top-ranked US universities, focusing on the relationships between departments within each institution. By applying complex network analysis, we identified the characteristics of successful partnerships and the qualities of effective research departments within these networks. Our findings revealed that networks with higher centrality and fewer isolated components tend to produce more innovative research, while also attracting greater funding. Additionally, we found that departments operating in isolated components produce fewer innovative contributions and generate less funding. Furthermore, we discovered that the knowledge stockpile of these departments often declines over time, suggesting a potential erosion of their research capabilities. Our study provides a framework for universities to evaluate and improve their research networks, fostering stronger partnerships that drive innovation and success. To this end, we introduce the concept of NRP -- Network Research Production function -- which can be used by universities to assess and optimize their research networks. By applying this concept, universities can prioritize their departments based on their research capabilities, knowledge maintenance, innovation productivity, and potential for cross-disciplinary collaboration. Our methodology enables the practical application of these ideas by providing a suitable framework for the analysis of academic partnership networks. Ultimately, our research can assist policy makers in designing targeted policies that promote innovative research production within these networks. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect (YORP) significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by gradually increasing their spin rate over time. By thoroughly examining asteroid three-dimensional spin states and mass estimates, the cause of accelerated spin down in (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro is attributed to the YORP effect, with (1620) Geographos' data not fitting YORP predictions. Various YORP sources contribute to this effect, with the most prevalent being the solar irradiance difference experienced as an asteroid orbits the Sun. By modeling their light curves and rotational velocities, the YORP values for (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro were calculated, with results showing their YORP values are positive. In approximately 100 years, (10115) 1992 SK's rotational velocity will increase sufficiently to display two maxima in light curve measurements, which will provide valuable opportunities for YORP effect studies. A practical YORP-driven binary asteroid candidate, (1698) Christoffel, with a close orbital path, faces a similar situation but will require much longer YORP influence before its light curves show the desired YORP effects. A practical approach to identifying YORP-driven rapid rotators among asteroids is also established in this study. A distinction is drawn between typical, slow-spinning asteroids and those experiencing the YORP effect, resulting in accelerated spin down, which will eventually manifest as permanent light curve patterns or primary-secondary mass ratio discrepancies. Our research provides a foundational understanding of the corrective learning process in robots and raises important questions about the fundamental properties of such methods. While HHL's potential is vast, implementing it is challenging due to high quantum state preparation costs. This research introduces seven new variations of HHL, designed to overcome such obstacles, by combining HHL with classical approximations, quantum random walks, and entanglement-assisted decoding, to take advantage of near-term quantum devices' ability to perform parallel circuit evaluations. These proposals focus on reducing quantum resources required, incorporating multiple noise-tolerant quantum subroutines, and integrating classical post-processing of partial solutions to offer higher-performance HHL variants. Simulation-based evaluations showcase how these proposals can enhance HHL's performance on noise-sensitive scenarios and offer more substantial performance gains than conventional HHL, despite requiring the same quantum resources. These proposals provide a blueprint for developing applications that can leverage near-term quantum hardware, capable of complex computations through modular, decentralized quantum classical collaborations. By employing a bijection established by Yang and Yang, researchers have access to a comprehensive understanding of UPSs. Building upon this foundation, a parametric variant of the Yang-Yang bijection is constructed, demonstrating its equivalence to a specific system of recursive equations. This construction facilitates the derivation of explicit formulas for frequency counts of UPSs, revealing intriguing patterns that mirror asymptotic properties of random parking configurations. Research into neutron detection is driven by the growing need for accurate detection systems in applications such as medical radiation treatment, nuclear safety surveillance, and security checkpoint screening. While rich information content can be obtained from neutron energy spectra with spectrometric detectors, such as time-of-flight and pulse-height analysis, there is a need to correlate detected signals with actual cross-sectional areas of scintillator materials. This work presents a novel 3D scintillator detector design and the development of a data analysis technique allowing for full-dimensional data interpretation. By demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach at the FRM II research reactor using a 65 MeV neutron beam, it has been shown that this detector design and analysis method can accurately determine neutron energies and cross-sectional areas with a margin of less than 25%. Furthermore, this study has determined the most sensitive parameters for neutron energy reconstruction and demonstrated the versatility of this detection system by utilizing it in conjunction with different neutron moderators. Additionally, this study has obtained a comprehensive set of neutron cross-sectional area measurements, which have been made available publicly, contributing to the global assessment of neutron cross-sectional areas. Furthermore, this study has also assessed the performance of this detector system using simulations, with the designed prototype demonstrating its ability to accurately determine neutron energies and cross-sectional areas in simulations involving complex geometries and multiple neutron scatterings. Overall, this work has validated the effectiveness of full-dimensional data analysis for neutron detection and has made available a comprehensive set of cross-sectional area measurements, which can be utilized in medical radiation treatment, nuclear safety surveillance, and security checkpoint screening applications. Furthermore, this study has also opened up possibilities for the utilization of this detector system in imaging applications that require accurate cross-sectional area measurements, such as photon-induced electron spin resonance imaging, by demonstrating its ability to accurately determine full-dimensional neutron energy spectra. Additionally, this study has also investigated the feasibility of upgrading this detector system to use a fiber-optic light guide, which has shown promising results in simulations involving complex geometries and multiple neutron scatterings, with this upgraded system having the potential to achieve even better performance. Overall, this work has provided valuable insights that can be utilized to design and develop more advanced and sensitive neutron detection systems in the future. Furthermore, this study has also demonstrated the ability of this detector system to accurately determine full-dimensional neutron energy spectra and cross-sectional areas, which has made it an ideal candidate for the detection system for the proposed photon-induced electron spin resonance imaging system. However, those studies overlooked the impact of temperature on particle sticking. To address this gap, the current experiment involves subjecting particles to high temperatures, simulating their journey deeper into a disc. As a result, the surface materials of the particles undergo significant changes as they move from the colder outer regions to the hotter inner regions. When exposed to high temperatures, the particles experience a range of changes in their sticking properties, with some displaying a more pronounced response than others. While the particles with the greatest temperature range experienced the greatest change in sticking forces, the influence of the particles' initial composition should not be overlooked, as the influence of water in this context was particularly notable. Water played a crucial role in the particles' behavior at high temperatures, with it becoming active above 1000 K and significantly enhancing the sticking forces by as much as 10 orders of magnitude. Researchers examined public Fermi-LAT data using machine learning techniques to identify blazars and other active galactic nuclei across the sky. Despite the extensive use of machine learning with Fermi-LAT data, a notable limitation exists in previous studies, namely the lack of spectral information for sources not aimed at Fermi-LAT. To address this, we compared models trained on all-sky maps with models trained on data with known characteristics, achieving significant accuracy in predicting source spectra. Our results show that by utilizing machine learning on Fermi-LAT data, including all-sky maps, we can accurately model source spectra in regions not previously analyzed. Furthermore, our analysis with the KNearestNeighbors algorithm revealed that sources with abnormal all-sky maps often correlate with sources exhibiting gamma-ray variability. Variability was observed in 25% of sources with abnormal maps, a significantly higher rate compared to their more conventional counterparts. Our analysis with the RandomForest classifier also highlighted that sources with abnormal all-sky maps frequently correspond with active galactic nuclei, specifically blazars, narrow-line Seyfert galaxies, and radio galaxies. In contrast, sources with conventional all-sky maps encompass a more diverse range of objects, including black holes, neutron stars, and mysterious objects like the magnetar TXP J173115+0034.2. Our study provides a foundation for large-scale machine learning applications with Fermi-LAT data, suggesting that such approaches can effectively identify variable sources in the sky. To facilitate further research, we made our model publicly available for comparison and improvement, accessible at https://github.com/astrosar/fermi-sar. Additionally, we presented the Sharpened All-Sky Chart, a comprehensive, machine learning-driven map illustrating the gamma-ray variability of sources across the sky, available at https://fermi-sar.github.io/sasc/. This resource is designed for researchers and astronomers to explore variable sources and facilitate future multi-wavelength studies. Furthermore, we provided recommendations for observing targets with current and upcoming telescopes, such as the Hubble Space Telescope, XMM-Newton, NuSTAR, and the X-ray Surveyor, as well as optical/near-infrared, radio, and optical counterparts, including GAIA satellite, VLA, Chandra, and the next-generation telescopes like the XMM-Omega B and the Athena. The Southern Atlantic rift system exhibits a unique and complex geodynamic history. Despite being the oldest continental margin rift system, geologists have a limited understanding of its early development phases. Studies have shown that a significant A~ndean-aged event shaped the South Atlantic, generating a linear and broad crustal basin. However, the South Atlantic rift system began developing during the C~mprian period around 560 million years ago. A team of researchers studied the J~ane/L~ongo ridge in western Brazil by collecting and analyzing fault rock samples as well as the geometry of faults at the rift's central and southern areas. Their data indicates that left-lateral shear occurred during the rifting process and suggests that it could have influenced first-phase extensional deformation in the central South Atlantic. Furthermore, strain localization in both the Jane and Longo areas occurred through the formation of a comprehensive network of faults with a N~e-N~eE orientation, often referred to as a rift-axis orthogonal pattern. This led to the creation of a triangular 'fissure' in the Jane area with a ~30 km short side. As rifting extended beyond the crust, it led to the formation of a ~20 km-wide and ~300 km-long igneous fault block in the central South Atlantic. This discovery has significant implications for models of continental break-up and the formation of large igneous provinces. It shows that continental rifting can occur beyond the crust and upper mantle, influencing processes r~ecorded in seismograms and causing the generation of large volumes of magma. It also suggests that pre-break-up stretching fields persisted until 150 million years after the continent had separated. It is also evident from kinematic analysis that extensional deformation in the central South Atlantic occurred in a non-uniform manner along a ~4,000 km axis, leading to the creation of a triangular 'fissure' in the Jane area and resulting in two distinct regions within the South Atlantic; an ~30 million-year-younger southern area with a broad and linear basin and an ~30 million-year-older central area that is a tri~angular 'fissure'. It is predicted that this difference in geometry could have an impact on oil and gas exploration in the two areas. It is also clear that left-lateral shear occurred during the rifting process and influenced first-phase extensional deformation in the central South Atlantic; however, it had no impact on second-phase deformation in the southern area. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with limited knowledge and skills, while the Dungeon Master represents a guiding intelligence tasked with leading them through a series of adventures. We create a multi-agent system based on natural language processing, which learns to manage player interactions and shape the story to come, and demonstrate its effectiveness through successful gameplay. Our approach serves as a robust evaluation of a learning agent's ability to interact with a rich, dynamic environment and navigate the complexities of social situations, as well as its capacity to follow rules and adapt to new information. We also find that incorporating a key aspect of human social cognition, known as Theory-of-Mind, enhances the Dungeon Master's performance and the overall quality of the gameplay it produces. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered that a simple single-factor constraint led to an overestimation of EDE's likelihood. As a result, its 95% confidence interval expanded to the range $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.029$ ($\chi^2$ profile likelihood) or $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.073\pm 0.030$ ($Bayesian") when comparing it to a $\Lambda$CDM model. As the EDE fraction is linearly related to the present-day effective neutrino mass, our findings imply a maximum of $0.036\pm 0.014$ eV for the effective neutrino mass at the 95% confidence interval. When incorporating the Hubble tension data, our results for the EDE fraction or effective neutrino mass cannot be fully reconciled with the predictions from the large-scale structure and cosmic microwave background alone. Additionally, we discovered that a two-factor constraint using the profile likelihood yielded more conservative limits on EDE than a single-factor constraint, but a Bayesian analysis produced a similar limit to the single-factor constraint. Conversely, when comparing it to a $\Lambda$CDM+H0 model, a two-factor constraint led to a marginally tighter limit on EDE, but with little impact on the effective neutrino mass. Similarly, the effective neutrino mass $m_\mathrm{nu}$ must be determined to better than $0.013$ eV. We introduce the concept of phrasal counterfactuals and develop a fine-grained classification task to study their detection. Counterfactuals express differences between two similar texts by highlighting altered segments. To demonstrate the feasibility of our approach with current language models, we establish the Counterfactual Classification Dataset (CCFD). This dataset comprises 12,352 counterfactuals and corresponding text pairs, gathered from 14 sources, including online forums and fictional story collections. Our evaluation reveals that both general-purpose and specialized models can accurately identify counterfactuals, but our proposed method surpasses their performance. To achieve this, we employed an ensemble of both supervised and unsupervised methods to construct a robust counterfactual classifier. Our results show that both the dataset and our classification technique are effective tools for analyzing and understanding the structure of counterfactuals. Additionally, we examine the relationship between counterfactuals and related concepts such as abstractions and causality, and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a case study involving the exploration of a fictional story dataset in reverse. Our research provides a starting point for the study of counterfactuals through large language models and datasets, and raises important questions about the potential applications of these models in complex tasks involving the exploration and understanding of complex textual narratives. Furthermore, we observe that a simple extension of our counterfactual classification algorithm can be used to identify the counterfactual status of individual phrases, allowing for both local and global counterfactual analysis. This has the added benefit of enabling the efficient construction of counterfactuals from scratch, based on the classification of individual phrase components. This in turn raises the possibility of developing a counterfactual generation module for existing language models, and we anticipate that future versions of these models will incorporate a counterfactual dimension, alongside aspects such as causality, morality, and semantics. This will, in turn, pave the way for the exploration of complex narrative datasets that convey counterfactual information, and will provide a common framework for the study of narrative texts that express abstract concepts. This, in the longer term, will lay the groundwork for the development of sophisticated narrative understanding capabilities in machines, and we anticipate that our counterfactual dataset and associated methods will play a key role in this ongoing effort. Furthermore, we believe that our results will also be of value to the broader community working on the evaluation and testing of natural language processing models, due to the novel nature of our counterfactual classification task, as well as the robust evaluation protocols that we have established

This study investigates the property of energy functions for the Miler-Deveney model, the Cattaneo model, and Caputo's model of order $\alpha$, $\alpha$ being between zero and one. These models are a fractional interpretation of the Allen-Cahn equation, and our analysis confirms that they possess a non-increasing energy functional, albeit only in the case when $\alpha$ is greater than five hundredths. For $\alpha$ equal to five hundredths, a modified energy functional is identified with a diminishing upper limit. Our research employs the technique of differential inequality, specifically the ODE approach to time-fractional differential equations. These results are valid across vast intervals. Additionally, we observe that both of these models admit a global bounded minimizer with the smallest energy value being zero. Our findings can be applied to time-fractional phase-field equations with non-normalized coherence type constraints. Our theoretical achievements are corroborated by numerical experiments. Our work suggests that models with $\alpha$ near zero but not actually zero may provide a viable alternative to the rigorous Allen-Cahn model. Our research also indicates that models with $\alpha$ near one but not actually one may be a suitable approximation to the classical Allen-Cahn model. Our study implies that models with $\alpha$ within this interval can serve as a flexible and effective tool for capturing classical sharp interface phenomena. Our work is further enriched by an extensive literature review highlighting both existing results and open questions. Our investigations are illustrated through an array of graphs, each presenting a relevant energy function over a given interval. Our results are applicable in both one and two-dimensional settings. Our findings are validated through a robust set of numerical experiments conducted using multiple initial conditions and conditions for the boundary. Our work in this paper is a significant contribution to the rigorous analysis of time-fractional phase-field models, overcoming previous limitations and providing a more comprehensive understanding of these models, their solutions, and their properties. Our research in this paper is a major advancement in the study of time-fractional differential equations and has the potential to impact not only the field of partial differential equations but also areas such as physics, geometry, and the study of differential equations in the context of curve and surface construction. Our achievements in this paper can also be seen as an important step in the analysis of time-fractional phase-field models and will likely have a lasting impact on the study of these models and their variants. The Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GSN) construction establishes an equivalence between groups representing states on C*-algebras and objects within the category of representation units, and this construction has numerous applications in quantum physics and poset theory. However, the Fock construction distorts this relationship, and distills the GSN construction into a pair of functors that map from the category of representation units to a related category of Hilbert space representations. We demonstrate that these functors form an adjoint pair, and we explore the implications of this relationship within the context of the Fock construction. Furthermore, we identify how this adjoint relationship arises from a unitary natural transformation known as the Haar measure, and we examine how this connection gives rise to a pair of 2-categorical units that link the Fock construction to the GSNG. Our findings are relevant to both the fields of quantum physics and poset theory. We primarily focus on the case of unitary representations, and we introduce new terminology, including the terms'state group' and'status group', to describe the objects within the category of representation units. Temporal sequence data, characterized by short sequences and high-dimensional observations, are increasingly used in life science studies, such as single-cell expression analysis and genomics, due to their ability to offer temporal knowledge, despite posing significant learning challenges because of their complex nature. Multivariate time series models like LSTM networks and GRU models have been effective in processing such data, albeit at the cost of extensive computational requirements and difficulty in interpreting results. Our proposed GuidedRNN model addresses these limitations by incorporating explicit temporal structure guidance from expert-provided temporal maps, facilitating more efficient and accurate learning from temporal sequence data. Through its integration of a novel optimization algorithm and robust estimation technique, GuidedRNN also offers an efficient and reliable performance across 13 real-world datasets, even in high-dimensional settings. Furthermore, we explore the practical applications of GuidedRNN through its incorporation into an analysis pipeline, demonstrating its effectiveness in life science studies, such as single-cell expression analysis and cancer diagnosis. Despite outperforming existing methods, GuidedRNN is characterized by a significantly more compact model size, making it an appealing alternative among the competing methods. The source code of GuidedRNN is publicly available on GitHub, at https://github.com/zhengwuhuang/GuidedRNN. Leveraging expert-provided temporal maps, GuidedRNN models short and high-dimensional temporal sequences by learning the underlying temporal structure, reducing both the computational requirements and the complexity of results. Through its efficient performance and robust estimation, GuidedRNN offers a more practical and flexible solution for life science studies. Additionally, we provide evidence that RNN-based models, like GuidedRNN, can capture the temporal structure from single-cell expression sequences, underscoring the potential of GuidedRNN to integrate this structure with genetic mutations data, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of cellular dynamics. Moreover, we demonstrate the versatility of GuidedRNN by assessing its capability to analyze cancer diagnosis and single-cell expression analysis, highlighting its efficient performance, robust results, and compact model size. Furthermore, we show that GuidedRNN can identify cancer subtypes and configure optimal hyperparameters through a combination of gradient-based and grid search methods, resulting in a leading performance among 11 competing methods. We analyzed a comprehensive database of molecular gas observations from 350 galaxies, focusing on the statistical properties of the CIA line at 809 GHz. Unlike previous studies, our analysis revealed that CIA line excitation does not follow a bimodal distribution, instead it is normally distributed. Conversely, the distribution of gas temperatures is skewed. Notably, the average temperature of 42 K is close to the value obtained from a normal distribution model of the CIA line. Our analysis indicated that one standard deviation of the CIA line distribution corresponds to a 16% standard deviation of the gas temperature. This threshold may be used to differentiate "hot" gas reservoirs. Additionally, we found that galaxies with "hot" molecular gas tend to have "hot" nuclear environments. Furthermore, "hot" gas reservoirs are associated with "hot" surrounding intergalactic medium, and are more common in dense galaxy groups. Conversely, "hot" gas reservoirs are less common in massive galaxies. "Hot" gas reservoirs are also less common in galaxies with stellar masses less than 10^10 M_⊙. Notably, the excitation of the [CII] line is only loosely linked to CIA line stimulation. Our analysis suggested that the main cause of CIA line stimulation is a non-uniform gas distribution, and that it may be used as an indicator of multi-component gas morphology. Conversely, the [CII] line stimulation is primarily caused by gas temperature variations. Our analysis indicated that the brightness of both the CIA and [CII] lines are strongly linearly correlated. Conversely, the [CII] line is about 2.5 times brighter than the CIA line. Our analysis suggested that the CIA line may be useful as an observational proxy for the total molecular gas mass when observing galaxies with "normal" gas temperatures. Conversely, if a galaxy has a "hot" gas reservoir, using the [CII] line as a mass estimator is more accurate. Our analysis also predicted the non-detection of the CIA line by the Herschel-SPIRE instrument at a flux density threshold of 0.56 Jy. This corresponds to a velocity-integrated line brightness of 1.4 Km/s. This report outlines our approach to addressing the MIR1K challenge's musical instrument recognition task, specifically in scenarios where only limited data is available for a particular instrument. We began by classifying instruments for which we have substantial training data and then focused on developing a protocol to recognize new instruments with little training information. Leveraging a hierarchical framework known as the Hierarchically Relational Prototype (HeRP), we trained both a high-level super-protocol and individual protocols for each instrument category. Our results revealed that HeRP outperforms alternative prototype-based methods and that our method's performance directly correlates with the within-category diversity of novel instruments, as assessed through a newly devised metric called the Category Diversity Index (CDI). Moreover, we observed HeRP's capability to generalize across various dataset splits and was even capable of achieving exceptional performance on MIR1K test sets with only partial access to the training data. Notably, our approach achieved top ratings in all three tracks of the MIR1K challenge. We also explored methods to enhance our HeRP model's performance on challenging instruments, incorporating additional features and conducting a comprehensive analysis of the impact of category diversity, all of which was facilitated by the HRP model's hierarchical nature. Finally, we experimented with a range of methods to tackle the few-shot learning setting, including the use of novel data with limited information about new instruments, and our code is now freely available for the broader research community to utilize. Additionally, we introduced a new challenge called the Few-Shot Instrument Sound Classification (FSISC) challenge, which poses a classification problem where only limited data is available for each instrument category, and we openly release our model's predictions on this benchmark as well. Our approach ultimately yielded the best performance across all tracks of the MIR1K challenge and ranked second in the FSISC challenge, according to the official evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we probed the performance of our model through comprehensive qualitative analysis, including both visual and auditory examinations, which provided further insight into its capabilities and areas for further improvement. Overall, our results demonstrate the exceptional performance of HeRP in instrument recognition tasks, and we are confident that this model will be a valuable resource for addressing a wide range of sound classification challenges across the music information retrieval domain. Furthermore, we strongly believe that our investigation into the principles underlying HeRP's success will also be beneficial in guiding the further development of prototype-based few-shot learning methods. The rapid dissemination of mathematical models for epidemic spread, particularly SARS-CoV-2, has led to a diverse range of predictive tools, but a critical examination of their underlying principles is long overdue. This paper seeks to reframe models as manageable approximations that emphasize analytical tractability over strict scientific accuracy, highlighting the established practice of compartmental modeling. We explore the benefits of SEIR models over simpler models, emphasizing the importance of asymptomatic individuals in model interpretation, before delving into the limitations of model fitting and forecasting. Finally, we discuss the value of models in informing policymaking and shaping public perception, urging researchers to prioritize transparency, reproducibility, and clear communication in both methodological choices and results. Furthermore, we propose a framework for collaborative, real-time analysis to address the complex challenges posed by emerging epidemics. This framework could be adapted for use on dedicated websites or platforms, facilitating the exploration of diverse methodological approaches and facilitating a deeper understanding of the epidemiological implications of model predictions. Ultimately, we must prioritize a holistic approach, combining scientific expertise and statistical modeling to guide the development of effective, evidence-driven policies that mitigate the spread of infectious diseases. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions fall short, and there remains a significant opportunity to develop a comprehensive, user-friendly platform that leverages the expertise of the academic community to address the complexities of acronym recognition and disambiguation. To address this gap, we present MadDog, a web-driven system built with a focus on user interactivity and powered by an extensive dataset compiled from MadAmI, aimed at enhancing the understanding of acronyms through related phrases, ontological structures, and contextual definitions. Although initially tailored for English acronyms, the system also caters to French acronyms, leveraging similarly constructed datasets. To facilitate continuous improvement, an associated application program interface (API) is provided for the integration of third-party modules, enabling MadDog to expand its capabilities in processing and interpreting acronyms across different domains and language variations. Furthermore, the system boasts an advanced user interface, allowing users to interactively explore acronyms, monitor system performance, and manage the underlying knowledge base. The system's source code is openly available for further development and customization. To utilize the MadDog system, a web-driven interface can be accessed at https://maddog.acronym.io, and the underlying code repository is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/acmrresearch/MadDog, under the permissive Open Source License (Apache License 2.0). Consequently, MadDog is poised to become a pioneering platform for developing acoustic models tailored to acronym recognition and disambiguation tasks. As such, the system may also find utility in acoustic model annotation tasks. In the open-world context, systems must operate effectively even if they don't have complete, up-to-date information about their environment. For critically used software, this implies the need for uncertainty modeling to ensure that critical decisions are made with appropriate caution. Given the complexity of real-world systems and their interconnected components, software engineers need practical tools to help with the process of calibrating uncertainty models to meet specific safety standards. To address these challenges, we present a general framework for modeling discontinuous uncertainty based on energy functions, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of using a specific implementation, tailored to logical programming, for calibrating uncertainty models in an open-world setting. The technique we present is applicable to a broad class of applications and can be easily integrated into the existing development process of software engineers. The proposed method has been successfully tested using a case study for navigation in an urban environment. The implementation of the technique in the form of a protocol can be used as a plugin for the existing development process, as can the case study, which has been incorporated into the Assure framework available at https://assure.seas.upenn.edu. The framework provides an uncertainty-modeling framework suitable for (semi)-automated use in the development of high-reliability software and showcases the technique through a demonstration of the protocol's application to the case study. The implementation of the framework can be accessed through https://github.com/usnmr1/assure-gh. The protocol for the method, along with the case study and the implementation of the framework, is currently being used in an ongoing research project aimed at developing a tool for predictive certification in the development process of software. The tool is designed to provide a way to automatically generate evidence for certification, as well as to assess the validity of the model in a dynamic environment. The tool is an enhancement of the Rascal framework, but with a new language that is more expressive and better suited for energy-based models. The enhanced version of the framework, along with the tool, is available for download. In systems with multiple timescales, the interaction between plant and animal populations follows a similar pattern, where plants grow quickly and then slowly decline as they age, while animals rapidly deplete their resources and then gradually rebuild. This phenomenon prompts an investigation into the long-term fluctuations and early warning signs of significant population changes in these ecosystems. By analyzing a mathematical model representing this relationship, our analysis reveals that the variability in the population's behavior is eventually determined by the model's lowest-frequency oscillation and its response to a threshold-based mechanism. Additionally, we identify specific indicators in the model that can signal the population's transition to an alternative equilibrium. These indicators include a measure of the population's distance from its initial state, the rate at which the population is changing, and a measure of the population's disorder. Interestingly, in some cases, the population's behavior can be controlled by a smaller subset of these indicators, demonstrating the complex interplay between the population's dynamics and its underlying structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the population's order can also serve as an early warning indicator for sudden changes, such as those caused by the death of multiple plants within a short period. This finding holds significant implications for our understanding of the population's behavior and can contribute to the development of more effective management strategies in ecosystem management. These research findings can also be applied to a related scenario involving the population's response to environmental changes, such as the death of plants due to a sudden drought. Building on these research outcomes, we propose a method for further exploring the population's dynamics in response to external influences and identify areas for growth in this line of research. Moreover, we establish a clear vocabulary for discussing the population's behavior, its internal structure, and the early warning indicators of significant changes, providing a theoretical foundation that can be used to study a broader class of models representing two-timescale ecosystem scenarios. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for investigating more complex, real-world applications, such as the management of forest ecosystems. Determining whether starbursts occur in gas-rich, merger-driven interactions or due to other factors has been a longstanding debate in the study of galaxy evolution. According to the Morophologically Selected Starburst Sample, typical starbursts result from major mergers, but there is a subset of starbursts, characterized by high mass-to-light ratios and low 4000A break strengths, that exhibit enhanced star formation rates relative to their mass. These exceptional starbursts are found at the high-mass end of the starburst population and are significantly overdensed. They are also distinguished by large central bulge masses and bulge-to-total mass ratios, as well as enhanced nuclear activity. These characteristics, combined with their dense cores, lead to enhanced starburst activity in this subset, causing a dip in the starburst SFR-mass relation at the high-mass end. Our research indicates that the turnover in the starburst SFR-mass relation observed by M*-SFR can be attributed to the presence of massive bulges. These bulges act as gravitational collapse centers, focusing mass in their nuclei and fueling extreme starburst activity. Our findings imply that the local dark matter potential plays a crucial role in governing the behavior of these bulges, resulting in enhanced nuclear activity, bulge growth, and an altered host galaxy. As a result, these galaxies exhibit unique properties, such as central dark matter dominance, strong nuclear domination, and overdensed hosts. Our research further reveals that these massive bulges can grow through a process known as "bulge-up" formation, caused by the collapse of dense dark matter filaments, induced by tidal interactions with an accompanying massive companion. These interactions resulted in the formation of twisted, spiral gas structures, fueling ongoing nuclear starburst activity in these galaxies. Consequently, these galaxies will eventually transition from starbursts to low surface brightness dwarf galaxies. Our research also allows us to interpret the observed turn-over in the starburst SFR-mass relation at high masses, and suggests a new, more extensive morphology-selected sample of starbursts that can be used to examine the local universe's galaxy population. These galaxies are found to inhabit a distinct region of the morphological selection starburst plane, separated from typical starbursts by their massive bulge-dominated nature. Our research implies that this subset of starbursts contributes significantly to the observed slow down of the starburst function at high masses, and that they are compact, bulge-dominated dwarf galaxies. Recently, researchers have made significant improvements to this theorem. For instance, the case of sums of four elements was solved by Erdos and R. R. Shapira further improved this by showing that if A and B share a sumset of size 3k-4, then A and B exhibit similarity to arithmetic progressions of length at most 4.095^k. We find that if the underlying fBm has a specific parameter and is shifted by a non-degenerate linear function, then the resulting process will have a non-empty interior. Additionally, if the shift function has a positive determinant and is compatible with the fBm's self-similarity parameter, then the resulting process will have a positive Lebesgue measure. Our research also identifies cases where analysis based on the reachability set is more effective. This leads to a scenario where the power to which the fBm is raised to a non-integer power affects its snapshots' properties. This research's findings are validated through numerical modeling. X-ray images contain valuable information that can be used to forecast whether a patient with COVID-19 will require intensive care unit (ICU) admission based on their chest radiology reports. By analyzing both visual features of X-ray images and clinical data, a combination of deep learning techniques and machine learning algorithms can be effective in predicting the need for ICU admission. To establish a more reliable model, exploring intuitive image characteristics and gathering expert opinions from radiologists are crucial steps. Furthermore, given the shortage of dedicated COVID-19 datasets, using transfer learning and building a diverse data set with various case presentations are key considerations. We propose a multi-stage model that leverages a pre-trained convolutional neural network and employs a simple feature extraction approach to predict the need for ICU admission from X-ray images and clinical information. We also examine the relationship between visual features of X-ray images and the likelihood of ICU admission. By examining 5000 cases from 12 hospitals, our findings demonstrate that there is a clear distinction in lung pattern between mild and severe cases, and certain pattern distributions correlate with the risk of ICU admission. Our model and research contribute to addressing the critical shortage of healthcare professionals and can assist in prioritizing COVID-19 patients in need of immediate medical attention. Neural models for playing chess and other strategy-based games efficiently have seen significant advancements in recent years. Unlike neural networks for other tasks, neural game agents aren't typically evaluated on their ability to generate code - instead, they're assessed through their performance in actual games against human opponents and other machines. This apparent disconnect may be attributed to the widespread practice of training neural game agents using self-play methods that bypass code generation altogether. This paper proposes a more nuanced view of neural game agents, acknowledging that many can be trained to generate high-quality code directly. We demonstrate this capability in the context of the AlphaZero chess model and show that models fine-tuned for code generation can achieve notable gains in playing strength when compared to their original counterparts. Furthermore, we find that models trained from scratch to generate code can match the expertise of those trained through self-play in just a fraction of the time required for self-play training. These findings suggest that evaluating neural game agents through code generation offers a valuable, more versatile means of assessment. We also explore various code generation metrics and evaluation protocols, along with techniques for training models to generate correct positions (states) and next moves (actions) simultaneously. Our work provides a new framework for understanding and advancing neural game agents and opens up opportunities for applying neural code generation models in a wide range of application domains. In addition, we introduce the concept of "evaluation graphs," a visual representation of game tree search processes that can be interpreted through code generation. We anticipate that this new view of neural game search will spark novel research directions, such as using attention mechanisms within evaluation graphs and developing multi-game code generation models that can easily adapt to new game domains with distinct rule sets. Cloud conditions are crucial for aircraft to maintain safe operating distances and effectiveness.  Currently, pilots rely on visual assessments of clouds to make these decisions, but this can be error-prone and time-consuming.  Automating the process would be advantageous, but requires a robust method for analyzing cloud conditions from images.  This processing step is often accomplished using deep learning-based approaches on pre-labeled datasets.  However, developing such datasets with comprehensive classifications proves challenging due to the diverse nature of cloud formations and the difficulty of standardizing classification schemes.  To address this issue, we introduce the WeatherCats dataset, which consists of 12,000 high-quality images spanning 13 categories and includes multiple views of clouds from various distances.  To enhance the performance of cloud-condition classification models, we propose a data augmentation technique called PatchRepeating, which outperforms existing methods.  Our findings demonstrate that PatchRepeating yields superior results on WeatherCats and other cloud-related datasets, while providing a more plausible visual representation that mimics the recurring patterns found in cloud formations.  Furthermore, we investigate the efficacy of various deep learning models and provide structured evaluations to provide valuable insights for future cloud-related computing research.  Our comprehensive evaluations showcase the superiority of PatchRepeating and the WeatherCats dataset, which we make publicly available to facilitate advancements in this field.  Overall, our research demonstrates the potential for significant improvements in cloud-condition classification through enhanced datasets and innovative deep learning techniques.  As such, we encourage the exploration of novel, sophisticated models that can capitalize on the complexities of these datasets.  As cloud-condition classification holds important implications for remote robotics and other safety-critical applications, we expect our contributions to contribute meaningfully to the advancement of this field. Open-domain conversation systems are highly sought after due to their potential to create engaging and dynamic interactions. These systems can be designed to operate in both closed and open-world settings, with the former involving pre-defined roles and the latter requiring the ability to adapt to new subjects of conversation. This paper proposes a method for constructing conversation systems that can handle a variety of topics and roles beyond what was initially programmed, leveraging large-language models such as BART and T5. By incorporating a role-based conversation framework and fine-tuning large-language models through a referral-based training process, we successfully developed a system that can engage in natural and coherent conversations in multiple roles and settings. Our system's effectiveness was validated through both automated testing and human evaluations, with results including: (1) role preservation, with the system correctly maintaining its assigned role in 86.1% of cases; (2) user experience, with human assessors finding the system's conversations both natural (N=4: 7.5/10, s=0.5; N=3: 7.3/10, s=0.1) and coherent (N=4: 8.3/10, s=0.3; N=3: 8.7/10, s=0.5); and (3) diversity, with the system generating over 8 different response types in over 80% of cases. Additionally, our method for constructing multi-role conversations was found to be efficient, with data preparation taking roughly one week for 10 roles and 10 subjects. The system we developed is available at https://github.com/yonrun/open-domain-conversation-system and is based on the Converse v2.0 dataset, with code modified from the Parsnav suite. Furthermore, we conducted a thorough analysis of system design, with findings that: (1) pre-trained models are necessary for open-domain conversation systems; (2) role preservation is crucial; and (3) diversity in response production is essential. In conclusion, our method offers a cutting-edge approach for constructing conversation systems that can operate in open domains and adapt to new subjects and roles. Additionally, we established that systems of this type should be designed with the ability to learn from multiple sources and incorporate a variety of topics and roles. Finally, we believe that further research is necessary to fully develop the capabilities of open-domain conversation systems, with potential applications including, but not limited to, virtual assistants, customer service platforms, and entertainment platforms. They found that matter falls onto the shock wave at a rate related to the density of the cosmos, contrary to previous models which assumed this relationship was proportional to the square of the density. By analyzing the impact of a radiative accretion disk on the inner region of the cavity, they found that it may disrupt the shock wave if the accretion rate is high enough, potentially affecting major processes of supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies. This scenario may also be applicable to other compact objects surrounded by an expanding cosmos. Researchers also discovered a condition to stabilize the shock wave and the cavity's temperature. If the accretion rate exceeds a certain threshold, the inner region's temperature will increase instead of decreasing, leading to a brighter X-ray spectrum. While related, these data measure distinct aspects of animal behavior, with capture-recapture data indicating occurrence and density within specific areas, and resource selection functions pinpointing preferred areas of use. When analyzed together, they can provide a more comprehensive understanding of population dynamics. However, combining these data types is complicated by different model parameters and a lack of standardization in data collection methods. To address this challenge, we developed a statistical model that incorporates both types of data, utilizing a conditionally autoregressive model for density estimation and incorporating habitat selection model parameters as a preference index. By applying this model to data collected in Alaska, we demonstrated that it can effectively account for density estimation and facilitate comparison of relative density values among study areas. Furthermore, we found that capture-recapture data alone may not accurately capture the variability of density estimates. Evaluating soccer team performance is a complex task, and analyzing their future behavior is even more complicated due to the ever-changing nature of the game's variables. Historically, sports analysts have employed linear and nonlinear statistical models to assess past performance, but these approaches fall short when predicting future outcomes. To further enhance this model's capability, we incorporated additional factors, including the location of the match being played, an element that previous studies have overlooked. By applying this model to data from the 2020 and 2022 European Football Championships, we discovered that home-field advantage has a significant impact on outcome, resulting in a 13.69% and 11.84% boost in the host team's chances of winning respectively. Furthermore, our research facilitated in-depth geographical analysis of the teams' performance, revealing correlations between a team's origin and their level of performance. Additionally, we identified groups of countries that consistently demonstrated similar levels of performance in various match scenarios. Recurrent extensions to traditional state space models hold significant value in analyzing time series data with broken patterns. However, existing approaches relying on observable state variables face limitations when attempting to model situations where the underlying dynamics are unknown and can't be directly observed. To address this challenge, we develop a novel framework that introduces latent variables to model dynamic changes and incorporates their effects on observable state variables through recurrent state space models. Our framework provides a Bayesian estimation methodology and an iterative algorithm for parameter inference. Moreover, we showcase the utility of this framework within the context of multi-step forecasting, leveraging observed data and prior knowledge to predict future observations. Notably, we apply this framework to a seminal economics problem, offering solutions for forecasting real variables in presence of an expectations formation process. Our methodology serves as a discursive tool to interpret general multi-state models and facilitates connection to established approaches like VAR and factor models. We complement our theoretical contributions with numerical experiments and economic case studies, highlighting the benefits of concealed parameter recurrent state space models in comparison to conventional approaches. Our results demonstrate superior performance of our proposed framework in forecasting scenarios and present a valuable extension of state space models suitable for modeling complex, hidden dynamic processes. This framework is also adaptable for use with modern deep learning architectures, enabling potential applications across various research domains. An accompanying R package named CRSSP is available for public access, enabling replication of our findings and facilitating users' access to our developed algorithms. This package can be installed via the official R repository. Leveraging the versatility of state space models and recurrent learning, we explore potential applications of this framework within the context of econophysics, forecasting, and time series analysis. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive overview of models derived from concealable parameter recurrent state space models in an accompanying appendix. This appendix is also a testament to the generality of this framework, as it yields innovative and efficient solutions to solve otherwise intractable problems of state space models. This, in turn, allows us to reconnect previously disparate models and provide a unified perspective on several well-known approaches within the field of time series analysis. This knowledge can be further utilized to design and develop novel models capable of handling complex, hidden dynamic processes. We anticipate this framework to contribute positively to the development of future models within the field of time series analysis. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. This architecture allows multiple tasks to be learned in an a task-conditioned manner, even when there is no explicit task identification information available. Experiments demonstrate that HyperPrompt outperforms current state-of-the-art models like Prompt-Tuning and Task-C conditioned Transformers in cross-lingual and few-shot learning settings. Furthermore, HyperPrompt shows significant gains over these models when the dataset is limited. We also find that HyperPrompt's HyperPrompt HyperNetwork is capable of selecting optimal task-conditioning through self-prompts, even in the absence of explicit target information. This is a notable finding because it suggests the possibility of a HyperNetwork-based approach for addressing data-free hyperparameter optimization. The source code for HyperPrompt is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/HyperPrompt. Additionally, model parameters for the tasks we evaluated are available upon request. We hope this work sparks further research on the integration of HyperNetworks and prompt-based learning to enhance the performance of Transformers in multi-task learning scenarios. The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the vulnerabilities of modern societies to global health crises and highlighted the importance of developing robust, adaptable, and resilient infrastructure for critical academic and research endeavors. In response to pandemic-related restrictions and the shift to remote work, many research organizations, including those in the United States, adopted remote work policies. This forced the acceleration of existing plans to develop remote work capabilities, leading to a significant expansion of user centers and a resulting need to manage and monitor large numbers of experiments simultaneously. To address these challenges, a collaborative team of researchers introduced a cutting-edge machine learning platform that allows real-time, centralized monitoring of user experiments and provides data-driven strategic guidance for optimizing research operations. This novel approach, which combines artificial intelligence with robust, secure, and scalable architecture, facilitated a major expansion of the Argonne National Laboratory's LeRoy Collins Center without the need for additional on-site staff. By transforming user centers into fully decentralized, self-managing entities, this technology has paved the way for a more decentralized and resilient scientific infrastructure that can adapt to a rapidly evolving global landscape. In this paper, we outline the key components of this machine learning platform and its applications, and we provide a case study on its successful implementation at the Argonne National Laboratory's LeRoy Collins Center. Under Van Rhijn's guidance, Blaauw conducted initial research on these topics, which later became the foundation for his own groundbreaking work. In 1945, after Van Rhijn's death, Blaauw succeeded him as director of the laboratory and implemented a plan to systematize the study of open clusters, which had been a major interest of his own. This established the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory as a leading center for research in this field. In the 1950s and 1960s, the laboratory conducted extensive surveys of the northern sky through projects such as the Leiden General Catalogue and the Revised General Catalogue, which were both initiated during Van Rhijn's directorship. These catalogues, combined with the use of optical and radio methods, allowed the discovery of hundreds of open clusters and thereby significantly expanded the known population of these types of clusters. This chapter will explore how the ideas and plans laid out by Pieter van Rhijn and the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory in the first half of the 20th century contributed to the major breakthroughs in the field of open cluster research in the second half. It will also provide an overview of the laboratory's open cluster research conducted in the second half of the 20th century and the key contributions made by its staff members. Finally, it will discuss the laboratory's current status within the Astronomical Institute of the University of Groningen and its ongoing open cluster research projects. As deep learning methods continue to evolve and gain popularity, the growing need for thorough evaluation of these models has created an insurmountable challenge for existing single-machine evaluation frameworks. This paper proposes a novel region-based training approach for deep neural networks with model-parallel learning, enabling efficient and scalable reviewering. We showcase this approach through the development of Regional Reviewer Trainer (RRT), a cutting-edge Python framework centered around the popular TensorFlow framework. RRT wraps the Model Parallel Distributed Basic Processor (MPDB) processor developed by Google, and bridges the gap between data and reviewer APIs. With RRT, we explore a range of reviewer configurations and assess their performance, revealing substantial gains in training time. For instance, the Pytorch ResNet50 model, typically trained on a single GPU in approximately 90 seconds, can be trained on four GPUs in around 60 seconds when utilizing four regional reviewers. This framework is compatible with leading deep learning frameworks, including Pytorch, TensorFlow, and Keras. RRT is an open-source framework suitable for complex, high-performance evaluation tasks, including object detection, segmentation, and classification, and is readily available for use and adaptation. Additionally, we introduce an enhanced version of RRT, incorporating a distributed data loader, referred to as RRT+ (Multi-Region Reviewer Trainer). This enhanced implementation demonstrates an average review time reduction of 30% across various models and datasets. With RRT+ and four regional reviewers, we achieve a review time of approximately 60 seconds for the Pytorch ResNet50 model. This efficient review time is matched by leading reviewering methods, such as Distributed Reviewer, yet is accomplished with significantly fewer reviewers. We make available extensive evaluation results, alongside our implementation, for further comparison and improvement of model-parallel reviewering methods. Furthermore, we outline several promising directions for enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of RRT+ and similar reviewering approaches. To address this, we developed a system that can accurately predict walking pattern intentions and lower body state from electrical signals obtained from the brain's surface. Furthermore, we observed significant differences in brain activity signals among volunteers who preferred ambulating with different step frequencies. These findings could potentially enable the creation of advanced brain-controlled wheelchair systems that anticipate the user's walking pattern and state, and could also contribute to managing sleep apnea and other health disorders associated with prolonged sitting. Additionally, incorporating additional brain signals, such as those related to balance and walking, could also enhance the model's predictive accuracy. Notably, our results allow us to derive pairs $(a, b)$ that can be used to construct the sequence $x_n=a^{2^n}+a\cdot7^n+b^{2^n}$, which meets the criteria $x_n=1$ for all non-negative integers $n$. This solution technique relies on the properties of the ring of integers in fields of characteristic not two and leverages the use of conjugate pairs in these fields. Additionally, our work involves analyzing the factorization of the quadratic form $a^2+ab+b^2$ in fields of characteristic two and establishing a link between its factors and the powers of $7$. We establish an expression for $a$ and $b$ in terms of the conjugate pair $(\alpha, \beta)$ and provide a formula for the sequence $x_n$, along with an alternative method for determining whether $x_n=1$ based on the value of $\beta$. We also outline an approach for extending our findings to other fields and discuss the implications of our work for the sequence $x_n$. Finally, we offer some guidance for potential research directions arising from these findings. Additionally, we provide a glossary to clarify the definitions of various terms used throughout the article. Lastly, we include an appendix containing an alternative method for establishing one of the results presented in the article. This method relies on the use of modular forms and Ramanujan's eigenfiltering theorem. Although this method does not yield a general formula for $a$ and $b$, it does allow us to derive additional solutions for the sequence $x_n$ based on the theory of modular forms. This approach also raises further research questions regarding the application of modular forms to Diophantine equations. We anticipate that the study of these equations will lead to a deeper understanding of the properties of modular forms and may provide a new perspective on the relationship between Diophantine equations

A major issue in robotics and dynamics research is navigating uncertain terrain, particularly when the surface gives way to softer ground. To tackle this challenge, a monopod robot designed to jump and move around was modeled and simulated in an environment with varying levels of hardness, and the simulation was improved with a method that helps the robot adjust to unexpected changes in the terrain. The modified model included a stronger and more resilient monopod, improved sensors that provide more accurate readings, and a control system that includes features to prevent the robot from getting stuck and to reduce impacts by adjusting its landing technique. The updated model was tested against the original design in the softer terrain, leading to improvements in performance and reliability. The monopod's legs were also analyzed and a more efficient design was identified, and a comparison was made between a robot with a hard ground-based controller and one with a controller that adapts to the softer terrain, showing the advantages of the adapted controller in the softer terrain. The results demonstrate the potential for highly effective navigation in soft terrain with properly designed robots. The study also raises questions about the limits of performance that might be achieved with optimal design, and suggests a method for validating models against actual robot performance. The study's methods could be applied to other complex robot systems, and might provide a framework for addressing issues with control systems, dynamics, and sensing in robotics. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English corpus for comprehensive negation understanding. This diverse set of 14,032 questions, spanning 5 tasks and encompassing 19 distinct topics, demands that models not only grasp the plain meaning of a passage but also effectively navigate negated, ambiguous, and contradictory text. A landmark evaluation framework, featuring both automatic and human-assisted evaluation processes, has been established to gauge the performance of models in comprehending negation. Our preliminary findings, derived from conducting extensive experiments involving state-of-the-art models and a comprehensive negation span prediction task, will contribute valuable insights to the community. Moreover, to facilitate further research, we openly release CONDAQA for public access. Our work underscores the critical importance of formal expression in language, as well as the role it plays in shaping the semantics of natural language, which existing implicit knowledge must capture. Therefore, developing models with the ability to process CONDAQA correctly will be a significant breakthrough. Furthermore, we anticipate substantial potential applications for these models in multiple contexts, including but not limited to, conflict-aware text summarization, negation detection, and natural language generation tasks. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for an exciting new research direction, which we term "negation-aware" NLP. Within this scope, we propose several novel tasks and introduce the Negation-Aware Reasoning Task (NART), which we believe should serve as a standard for evaluating the capacity of models to grasp complex semantic concepts within natural language. NART embodies the ideal that models should be capable of understanding not just the surface-level content of a passage but also its underlying semantic structure, which is intricately linked to the notion of formal versus non-formal language. As such, we advocate for the adoption of a more expansive definition of natural language, which acknowledges the presence of formal language as a fundamental component, and we encourage the community to participate in our research effort. Lastly, we invite scholars to explore additional dimensions of negation across multiple languages and to consider collaborating with us. Additionally, we have released open-source code and leaderboards associated with CONDAQA, which can be accessed via our website. In the context of information networks, where the graph represents the posting schedule of topics and entities, and edges indicate co-occurrences, our study focuses on isolating groups of entities that jointly post frequently. To address this issue, we developed two scalable frameworks – one based on partitioning the graph along a dynamic timeline and another on a static timeline – which demonstrate superior performance and memory efficiency compared to existing approaches. Our proposals also offer enhanced accuracy and are particularly well-suited for today's distributed computing environments. Our experiments showcase the efficacy and efficiency of our methods, with the benefit of their open-source code available for public use. Furthermore, we anticipate our techniques to be valuable for various graph mining applications. In addition to presenting our methods, we explore theoretical aspects, including the implicit communication pattern of our algorithms and a complexity analysis of the clique computation problem. In line with previous research, we assume a shared memory environment and focus on finding solutions for specific graph substructures. Building upon prior work, we investigate various parameterized cases of the clique computation problem. Our study reveals that certain instances may be efficiently solved by our methods and, in some cases, the optimal solution requires a significant amount of memory. In the case of parameter k, we demonstrate that a clique of size k can be computed in O(k^3) time using a parallel approach. In the context of parameter treed, we show that a maximum weighted clique can be computed in O(t \* 4^t) time. In the case of parameter leaf, we demonstrate that a maximum weighted clique can be computed in O(l \* 2^l) time. In the case of parameter tree, we demonstrate that a maximum weighted clique can be computed in O(t \* 4^t) time. In the case of parameter path, we demonstrate that a maximum weighted clique can be computed in O(p \* 2^p) time. In the case of parameter wheel, we demonstrate that a maximum weighted clique can be computed in O(w^3) time. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics within quantum systems: annealing ensues from a ground state, whereas quenching generates highly excited states with, occasionally, converged results. The study of Heisenberg interactions to simulate Ising annealing has yielded inaccurate simulations due to insufficient system size, contrary to classical simulations. This research demonstrates the value of the quantum annealing interval in achieving ground state results with Heisenberg simulations, matching classical Ising simulations. Furthermore, various quenching scenarios result in an understanding of the parameters that contribute to successful outcomes with Heisenberg quenching. Both interval and quenching parameter findings contribute valuable knowledge for the development of quantum annealing protocols. Additionally, we explore the temporal dynamics that occur during both interval and quenching processes, shedding light on the behavior of quantum systems in relation to classical simulations. The principles derived from these investigations are applicable to solving other combinatorial optimization problems, as exemplified through the solution of an exact cover problem. The research employs Heisenberg simulations of annealing and quenching, involving Ising equivalents, including a novel approach to reproduce the outcomes of classical simulations. The study's findings provide a framework for the design of quantum annealing protocols, incorporating both interval parameters and quenching dynamics, to successfully solve complex computational problems. The developed protocol serves as a model for implementing quantum annealing algorithms, utilizing quantum systems to resolve peer-to-peer network connectivity problems. Furthermore, the research showcases the efficacy of Heisenberg simulations in deriving valuable insights into the behavior of quantum annealing and quenching, resulting in the development of an optimized quantum protocol. The proposed protocol is a connection strategy, dubbed 'Q-Path', designed to minimize the physical distance between connected Ising spins, facilitating the identification of coupled Heisenberg spins. The implementation of Q-Path, within a quantum system, is achieved through the incorporation of two additional spins per Heisenberg spin, effectively converting the Heisenberg model into that of coupled Ising spins. The resulting quantum circuit, incorporating the Q-Path connection strategy, serves as a model for the development of optimized quantum annealing and quenching protocols in solving complex computational problems. The study's findings are applicable to solving other exact cover problems, as demonstrated through the solution of a binary exact cover problem. The issued raised in this work also applies to quantum simulation of chemical reactions and other complex phenomena, highlighting the significance of the proposed solution.
